title: Same-Origin Policy and CORS
subtitle: Why your fetch fails cross-origin and how CORS allows it
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Without Same-Origin Policy, a script on evil.com could make requests to bank.com using your session cookies, read your account balance, and transfer money — all while you are on evil.com.
whyItExists.solution: The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) prevents JavaScript on one origin from reading responses from a different origin. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the standard mechanism for a server to opt-in and allow specific cross-origin access.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every time you build an API that will be called from a different origin. Every time you debug a 'CORS error'. Understanding SOP explains why the browser blocks certain requests and what to do about it.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: SOP is a browser security mechanism — it applies to browser-based JavaScript. Server-to-server requests are not subject to SOP.

explainModes.beginner: Imagine your browser is like a careful friend who carries your bank card. They will only use your card at the exact bank you told them — not at random shops that claim to be your bank. The Same-Origin Policy is your browser refusing to let scripts on one website read data from a completely different website. CORS is the mechanism a trusted website uses to tell your browser: 'Yes, you can share data with me.'
explainModes.simple: Same origin means: same protocol (https), same domain (kernal.dhurta.org), same port (443). Different origin = different any of these three. SOP rule: JavaScript can SEND cross-origin requests (with CORS or not), but can only READ the response if the server explicitly allows it via CORS headers. Without CORS: fetch('https://api.other.com/data') from your site returns a 'CORS error' — the request was sent and the server responded, but the browser blocked your JS from reading the response. Fix: the API server must add Access-Control-Allow-Origin header.
explainModes.standard: CORS works through HTTP headers. For 'simple' requests (GET/POST with simple content types), the browser adds an Origin header and checks the response for Access-Control-Allow-Origin. For 'non-simple' requests (custom headers, PUT, DELETE, JSON bodies), the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request to check whether the actual request is permitted — only proceeds if the preflight succeeds. CORS headers are set by the server, not the client. Setting CORS headers in your frontend code does nothing.
explainModes.technical: Preflight conditions: method is PUT/PATCH/DELETE, or Content-Type is application/json, or any custom header is present. The preflight OPTIONS response must include: Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers, and optionally Access-Control-Max-Age (cache duration for the preflight). Credentialed requests (cookies + CORS) require both Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true AND the client to set credentials: 'include' in fetch options AND the server must NOT use wildcard (*) in Access-Control-Allow-Origin — it must echo back the specific origin.
explainModes.deepDive: The same-origin policy has two important exceptions: scripts loaded via <script src=''> inherit the loading page's origin, not the script file's origin — this is why CDN-hosted JavaScript can run in your page context (and why you should use Subresource Integrity for CDN scripts). Forms can submit cross-origin (POST to a different domain) but cannot read the response — this is why CSRF exists and why CSRF tokens are needed. The CORB (Cross-Origin Read Blocking) extension to SOP in Chrome blocks sensitive cross-origin responses even from same-site iframes, preventing Spectre-class attacks that use side-channel timing.

content.code:
An origin is: protocol + hostname + port

https://kernal.dhurta.org/lessons    → origin: https://kernal.dhurta.org
https://kernal.dhurta.org/roadmap    → origin: https://kernal.dhurta.org  (same)
http://kernal.dhurta.org/            → DIFFERENT (http ≠ https)
https://api.dhurta.org/              → DIFFERENT (different subdomain)
https://kernal.dhurta.org:8080/      → DIFFERENT (different port)
https://otherdomain.com/             → DIFFERENT (different domain)

Two origins are the same only if ALL THREE parts match exactly.

content.text: JavaScript running on one origin can send requests to other origins, but it can only read the response if the server explicitly permits it with CORS headers.

content.code:
Server response to a cross-origin request:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://kernal.dhurta.org
  ↑ Only kernal.dhurta.org can read this response

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
  ↑ Any origin can read (OK for public APIs, NOT for auth)

Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
  ↑ These HTTP methods are allowed cross-origin

Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
  ↑ These request headers are allowed

Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
  ↑ Cookies will be included (requires specific origin, not *)

content.text: For non-simple requests (DELETE, PUT, or any request with JSON body or custom headers), the browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request first to ask the server if the real request is allowed.

CORS is a server-side configuration. If you get a CORS error, the fix is on the server — add the correct headers. Nothing you do in your frontend JavaScript can bypass SOP (and you should not want to — it protects your users).

questions.question: Your frontend (https://app.com) gets a CORS error fetching from https://api.com. Where is the fix?
options: In the frontend fetch() call — add a 'no-cors' mode
In the browser settings — whitelist the API domain
On the API server — add Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.com to responses
In the HTML — add a <meta> CORS tag to the frontend page
questions.explanation: CORS is a server-side configuration. The API server (api.com) must add the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header to its responses. Adding 'mode: no-cors' in fetch just makes the response opaque — you cannot read the data. There is no browser setting or frontend HTML that can bypass SOP (which is the whole point).

questions.question: When does the browser send a preflight OPTIONS request before the actual request?
options: For every cross-origin request without exception
Only for GET requests to check the server is alive
For non-simple requests: DELETE/PUT, custom headers, or JSON body
Only when the server requires authentication
questions.explanation: Simple requests (GET/POST with form data or plain text body, no custom headers) do not trigger a preflight. Non-simple requests do: PUT/DELETE/PATCH methods, requests with Content-Type: application/json, or any custom header (like Authorization). The browser sends OPTIONS first to confirm the server allows this type of cross-origin request before sending the real one.

faq.q: Why does my server-to-server request work but browser fetch fails?
faq.a: Same-Origin Policy is a browser security mechanism — it only applies to JavaScript running in a browser. When your Node.js server, curl, or Postman makes a request, there is no browser enforcement. Only browsers enforce SOP. This is why a proxy pattern works: your frontend fetches your own API (/api/proxy), and your server makes the cross-origin request on behalf of the browser — no CORS needed.

faq.q: Is CORS enough to secure my API?
faq.a: No. CORS controls which browser origins can read your responses. It does not authenticate users, authorize operations, rate-limit requests, or prevent server-to-server abuse. Think of CORS as browser-level access control only. You still need authentication (tokens, sessions), authorization (who can do what), input validation, and rate limiting.

examples: The most common beginner error: 'CORS error' when fetching a local backend from a different port — fix by adding CORS headers in your Express/FastAPI/etc. server
Public APIs like the GitHub API return Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * so any website can fetch public data
A CORS misconfiguration (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true) allows any site to make credentialed requests — a serious vulnerability
